Barclays Still Sees 100% Upside for Oracle. Here's How It Gets to $252 ©Garakta Studio from Garakta Studio via Canva
Key Takeaways

Barclays repeated its Overweight rating and $252 price target on Oracle on Oct. 26. That target is 100% above the stock's last close.

Barclays' case is that Oracle's cloud infrastructure growth keeps speeding up and its funding has improved, backed by a $664 billion backlog.

Oracle trades at 15x forward earnings, against a five-year average of 21x, and free cash flow is still negative.

Barclays' $252 needs about 30x next-twelve-months earnings, which looks out of reach within a year, though it's close to what Oracle's average multiple gives on fiscal 2028 estimates.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) has lost 56% since its closing high last October. Barclays still thinks it can double from here.

On Monday, Oct. 26, Barclays analyst Raimo Lenschow repeated his Overweight rating and $252 price target, 100% above Oracle's last close.

The cost of the build

In fiscal 2026 (the year to May 31, 2026), Oracle's capital spending hit $55.7 billion and its free cash flow was negative $23.7 billion. To pay for its AI data centers, Oracle sold $25 billion of bonds, $5 billion of preferred stock and $20 billion of common stock between February and August.

Then Oracle's Sept. 10 report showed another $5 billion of negative free cash flow, with $90 billion to $95 billion of capex planned for the year. Asked when free cash flow turns positive, CFO Hilary Maxson said, "We haven't given a particular time frame on that yet, and we don't expect to give that today."

How Barclays gets to $252

Barclays' case is that Oracle's growth has turned a corner and should keep speeding up, and that funding has improved. The quarter to Aug. 31 backs up the first part: cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% to $7.4 billion, and its backlog reached $664 billion. Management expects about half of it to become revenue within 36 months.

On funding, Oracle booked more than $30 billion of new AI contracts that management says won't require more capital from Oracle.

Does $252 add up?

The consensus target has fallen from about $350 a year ago to $237.

Targets run from $110 to $400, and Barclays' is just 7% above the average.

Earnings estimates are holding up. Analysts expect $8.14 of normalized EPS in fiscal 2027 and $10.99 in fiscal 2028, both a little higher than 90 days ago.

title: What Is The Market Seeing In Manhattan Associates Stock?

What Is The Market Seeing In Manhattan Associates Stock?
Trefis Team

Image from Pixabay

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Manhattan Associates (MANH) stock trades at 66.6 times its earnings over the last twelve months, compared with 22.9 for the S&P 500. Investors buying at that multiple are paying for growth the company has not shown lately. Revenue rose 6.5% over the four quarters to June 2026. So what growth are buyers paying for at this price?

How Fast Would Manhattan Associates Have To Grow?

At today's price, Manhattan Associates would have to nearly double its revenue over five years just for its shares to hold their value as its P/E settles lower, leaving no return on top for a buyer.

The company was worth about $14.0 billion at the October 23, 2026 close. To support that value at a P/E of 28.8, the business would have to earn $486 million a year, compared with $210 million over the last twelve months. At a net margin of 22.4%, it would have to sell $2.17 billion a year, up from $1.13 billion now. That margin sits above both the company's average net margin of 20.1% and its high of 21.4% over the last twelve quarters. Trefis allows five years when today's P/E is two to three times the assumed multiple, and here it sits at 2.31 times. Over those five years, the company would have to grow revenue 14.0% a year.

The P/E, the margin, and the five-year timeframe are Trefis assumptions. Trefis builds the P/E from a software industry level of 28.0, weighted at 60%, with the stock's own average P/E over the last twelve quarter ends making up the rest. That average was 61.7, so Trefis counts it at a cap of 30 instead.

Manhattan Associates' Cloud Business Outpaces Its Total Revenue

Buyers appear to be paying for the cloud business, where customers subscribe to the company's supply chain software on its Manhattan Active platform. Cloud revenue rose 26% to $127 million in fiscal Q2 2026, compared with 9.3% growth for total revenue. Management raised its fiscal 2026 cloud revenue forecast to $505.5 million at the midpoint, representing 24% growth. Revenue under signed contracts that the company has not yet recognized reached $2.47 billion at the end of June, up 23% from a year earlier.

Total revenue is growing more slowly. Management expects fiscal 2026 revenue of $1.160 billion to $1.166 billion, or 7.5% growth at the midpoint. After that year, Manhattan Associates would have to grow 14.8% a year through mid-2031, about twice the 7.5% it guided for 2026. Its long-standing aim is double-digit growth, but it has given no guidance for 2027 yet.

ServiceNow NOW is scheduled to release its third-quarter 2026 results on Oct. 28.

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for third-quarter revenues is currently pegged at $4.09 billion, indicating 20% growth from the figure reported in the year-ago quarter.

The consensus mark for earnings is pegged at $1.02 per share, unchanged over the past 30 days and indicating growth of 6.3% from the year-ago quarter.

Let's see how things are shaping up prior to this announcement.

NOW's Q3 to Ride on Strong Portfolio Amid Stiff Competition

ServiceNow's third-quarter 2026 results are expected to have benefited from accelerating enterprise adoption of agentic AI solutions, particularly Now Assist, AI Control Tower and Autonomous Workforce. The company's AI annual contract value (ACV) exceeded $1 billion in the second quarter, with net new AI ACV growing more than 40% sequentially. Growing AI deployments, combined with stronger customer consumption and increased adoption of higher-value AI packages, are expected to have supported subscription revenues.

NOW's new AI-native packaging strategy is expected to have boosted third-quarter performance by making AI capabilities accessible to a wider customer base. The company's Foundation, Advanced and Prime offerings allow enterprises to adopt AI based on their requirements. Increasing monetization opportunity is expected to have supported deal values and subscription growth. Moreover, sustained demand for IT Service Management (ITSM) and IT Operations Management (ITOM) solutions has been a key catalyst. In the second quarter of 2026, ITSM featured in 15 of the company's 20 largest deals, while ITOM was included in 18.

The company's expanding cybersecurity portfolio is expected to have been a significant contributor to third-quarter top-line growth. The integration of Armis and Veza strengthens NOW's capabilities in asset intelligence, identity security, vulnerability management and automated threat response. These solutions complement AI Control Tower and the existing ITSM and ITOM portfolios, creating opportunities for cross-selling. The combination is expected to have supported subscription revenues, larger enterprise contracts and greater adoption of the company's core workflow solutions.

However, ServiceNow's third-quarter subscription revenue growth is expected to have faced pressure from the timing of U.S. federal government contracts. Strong federal demand in the second quarter accelerated certain on-premises subscription revenues that would otherwise have been recognized in the third quarter. This pull-forward creates a difficult sequential comparison despite healthy underlying demand. NOW expects third-quarter subscription revenues of $3.975-$3.980 billion, indicating approximately 20% year-over-year growth in constant currency, compared with 23% growth in the second quarter.

The company's third-quarter results are expected to have suffered from unfavorable forex and acquisition-related charges. Higher AI processing requirements and cloud delivery costs are likely to have increased subscription costs. Moreover, stiff competition from Salesforce CRM, Microsoft MSFT, Oracle ORCL and other enterprise software vendors that are rapidly embedding generative AI into their platforms, requiring continued investment to sustain technological leadership, has been a headwind. This is expected to have kept margins under pressure in the to-be-reported quarter.

title: Microsoft Vs. Oracle: Massive Backlog Fortunes With Vastly Different Risk Profiles

Quick Read

Microsoft and Oracle both hit record backlogs near $678B, but Microsoft generated $19.64B in free cash flow while Oracle's heavy capex pushed it to -$5.40B.

Oracle fell 54% over the past year while Microsoft gained, with Oracle's 18x forward earnings multiple versus Microsoft's 25x reflecting higher balance sheet risk.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) each ended their latest quarter with a record backlog. Microsoft reported $678B in commercial RPO, and Oracle reported $664B. The two figures are close, but the money behind them is very different. Microsoft pays for AI capacity out of a highly profitable software business. Oracle is turning itself into an AI infrastructure landlord and relies in part on raised capital to do it.

24/7 Wall St.
Azure Throws Off Cash While Oracle's Cloud Burns It

Microsoft's fiscal Q4 revenue reached $90.01B, up 17.8%, and Azure grew 43%. Even after heavy spending, the quarter produced $19.64B in free cash flow, so the AI expansion is paying for itself. Copilot passed 30 million paid seats, which shows AI is earning money in Office as well as in data centers. CFO Amy Hood said "customer demand continues to exceed available capacity."

Oracle's cloud infrastructure revenue grew 121% in fiscal Q1, and GPU usage was 97.9%. Demand is clearly there. However, $28.50B of capex turned free cash flow negative at $5.40B. License revenue fell 15% as the older software base moves to the cloud.
